reason: Current fields are explicitly real-vector-valued maps, with coherent SI units assigned separately. The displayed amplitudes specify the numerical map components in those units. Their longitudinal numerical amplitude 1 denotes physical TE amplitude 1 A/m and physical TM amplitude 1 V/m. No arbitrary amplitude parameter is claimed or needed for these particular candidates.
limitations: No exact current source sentence says "all displayed formulas are numerical SI components"; this conclusion follows from the explicit mathematical codomains plus the adopted unit assignments, rather than quoting an absent convention.
The SI source uses quantity notation as well as numerical-value notation. Its quantity table does not override the explicit R³ mathematical types.
This is not a third repair, a new normalization restriction, or a changed public interface. No formal 5b verdict, receipt, approval rehash, or hold removal has been written.
If the owner rejects this reading, both primary subjects remain capped and held; there is no authorized content-repair path.
independent_argument: E and B are maps to R³, read componentwise in the laboratory orthonormal basis; P and M have the same codomain, and H=mu0^-1 B-M is thus another real-component field. Units are additional framework assignments, not an alternative codomain of dimensioned quantities.

SI conventions assign metres, seconds, V/m, T, A/m and the coherent material units. Writing q_phys=q_num*u_q reconstructs the physical quantity from the real map component and its assigned unit. This representation needs no new postulate or free scale.

For TE10, the numerical component H_z=cos(pi*x1/a) fixes the longitudinal amplitude to 1 in its assigned A/m unit. The physical electric prefactor is (omega_phys*mu_phys*a_phys/pi)*(1 A/m), whose unit is (V/A)*(A/m)=V/m. The displayed coefficient is its numerical value in V/m. Treating that coefficient as a quantity in V/A while treating the same formula H_z=cos as a physical quantity mixes numerical and quantity representations.

For the general TE reconstruction the physical longitudinal profile is (1 A/m)*h_mn. For TM it is (1 V/m)*e_mn. Differentiating numerical profiles in metre coordinates and multiplying numerical omega, mu or epsilon yields the same numerical reconstruction formulas because these SI units are coherent.

Energy/flux formulas use those particular already-fixed candidate map amplitudes; their numerical values carry J/m and W respectively. No extra arbitrary-amplitude factors are missing from a formula for these fixed candidates. Completeness statements use scalar profile spans/index exclusion, invariant under a nonzero fixed unit choice.

exact_public_source_sections.quote:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its units, its fields $E,B$ and its source densities $\rho,J$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], and let the averaging convention be that of [[post-em-coarse-graining]], in whose sense the objects below are macroscopic. Any convolution used to instantiate that reading is taken on its declared exact interior-footprint domain, or under a declared locally integrable compatible extension covering every used footprint. Its every-time use requires every-time locally integrable spatial slices; joint spacetime local integrability alone supplies only the almost-every-time branch. The joint $C^2$ regularity specified below is a separate model hypothesis, not a consequence of spatial smoothing.

**(a) [Polarization and magnetization]** The material model specifies two maps $P,M:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] on the open set $\Omega\times I$: $P$ is the electric dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $M$ the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, both read in the frame basis. They are data of the chosen material model: this definition does not compute them from $E$ and $B$, and no relation between $(P,M)$ and the fields is asserted here.

**(b) [Bound sources]** Write $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ for the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] taken at fixed $t$, and $\partial_t$ for the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] at fixed position, and define the bound charge density and bound current density by

$$\rho_b:=-\operatorname{div}P,\qquad J_b:=\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M.$$

Since $P,M$ are jointly $C^2$, $\rho_b$ and $J_b$ are continuous, indeed $C^1$, by the componentwise sum and product rules of [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]; $\rho_b$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and $J_b$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$.

**(c) [Free sources]** Define $\rho_f:=\rho-\rho_b$ and $J_f:=J-J_b$, in the same units as $\rho$ and $J$; these are the free charge and free current densities of the model. The decomposition $\rho=\rho_f+\rho_b$, $J=J_f+J_b$ is part of the chosen material model: the same total pair $(\rho,J)$ with a different pair $(P,M)$ is a different model.

**(d) [Displacement and magnetic intensity]** Define the electric displacement and the magnetic intensity by

$$D:=\varepsilon_0E+P,\qquad H:=\mu_0^{-1}B-M,$$

where $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0,c>0$ are the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; $D$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $H$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

**(e) [Status]** This item fixes objects and the bound/free convention only. No field equation (the item `pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell`), no constitutive relation (the item `post-em-material-closure`), no conservation of the bound pair (the item `pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell`, clause (a)) and no identification of $P,M$ with microscopic dipole sums is asserted here.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and define $\nabla_t f=(\partial_1f,\partial_2f,0)$, $\Delta_t f=\partial_1^2f+\partial_2^2f$ and $\operatorname{div}_tu_t=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2$ for the stated regularity, using [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].
(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\Omega_A:=A\times\mathbb R$ where $A$ is either a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) or the explicit rectangular cross-section; the rectangle has corners and is treated by its open faces, not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\{x_1=0\},\{x_1=a\},\{x_2=0\},\{x_2=b\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\Omega_c:=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. The separate smooth-cavity spectral branch uses an explicitly declared bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ with its smooth PEC boundary; it is not the rectangular reflection class. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\Omega\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.
(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $\sigma_f=-n\cdot D$ and $K_f=-n\times H$ for the filling-side traces (the wall normal points from the filling into the conductor, so the jump is $0$ minus the filling trace) are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\sigma\to\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.
(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\operatorname{div}E$ and $\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions. This is the declared weak PEC model used for the cavity initial-value problem; when the reflected extensions are continuous across the walls, their odd components vanish there, giving $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on the open walls. Smoothness only inside $Q$ does not imply this extension continuity. Initial data not in this class (for example data with trapped normal $B$) are excluded, as are the general $H(\operatorname{curl})$ boundary classes, which are defined by the mathematical suppliers and are not identified here with the classical conditions.
(d) [TE, TM, TEM] For a guide or cavity field $(E,B)$, the longitudinal components are $E_z:=E\cdot e_z$ and $B_z:=B\cdot e_z$; the field is called TE (transverse electric) if $E_z\equiv0$, TM (transverse magnetic) if $B_z\equiv0$, and TEM if both vanish, always relative to the named axis $e_z$.
(e) [Separated phasor convention] For $\omega>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb C$, a $\beta$-$\omega$ separated phasor field on the guide is a real field of the form $F(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with a complex amplitude $\tilde F$, componentwise; $\omega/(2\pi)$ is the frequency and $\beta$ the longitudinal propagation constant; when $\beta$ is real, $\beta>0$ describes propagation in the $+e_z$ direction under this phase convention, while a complex $\beta$ gives the spatial factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}\beta x_3}$ and may grow in the opposite direction; each consuming branch states its selection.
(f) [Scope] The definition fixes the geometry, the PEC boundary model, the weak reflection class and the mode terminology; it asserts no field equation, no constitutive law and no existence or completeness of modes, Rectangular TE/TM candidates and the rectangular reflection class, declared smooth bounded PEC cavity spectral classes, and smooth straight-guide TEM potential branches (including the coaxial annulus) are within this geometry. No general non-rectangular TE/TM guide theory, circular-guide spectral classification, open-end or junction scattering, or arbitrary lossy model is supplied. The same stationary PEC geometry also hosts the explicitly declared constant scalar Ohmic cavity class and the full longitudinal finite-energy reflection class of the straight rectangular guide; constitutive and evolution claims belong to their consuming theorems, not this definition.

**Conventions fixed by this definition.** The definition records objects and conditions only: the guide and cavity regions, their open walls and outward normals, the ideal PEC boundary conditions with their interface reading and excluded idealization, the zero-normal-$B$ reflection class with its distributional divergence constraints, the axis-relative TE/TM/TEM terminology, and the separated phasor encoding of real fields. It asserts no field equation, no constitutive relation, no existence, uniqueness or completeness of modes, and no dissipation or energy claim; those belong to the consuming theorems, each of which restates the branch of the material model it uses. The rectangular cross-section is treated through its four open faces and is not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, and no pointwise condition on box edges is made.

Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following constitutive branches for the material described by the macroscopic fields of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]].

**(a) [Material rest frame]** The relations below are stated in a material rest frame: an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the Minkowski model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$, hence history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$ on the declared time interval. When this is the laboratory frame, the components below are laboratory components. Boosting the material changes both the fields and the rest observer; this postulate does not assert that the relations below hold with the same constants in every frame.

**(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch]** In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes

$$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$

where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. For a real matrix $T$, symmetric means $T^{\mathsf T}=T$, positive definite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive semidefinite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv\ge0$ for every $v$. Entries of $\varepsilon,\mu,\sigma$ carry respectively $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\mathrm H\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\mathrm S\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, where $\mathrm F=\mathrm C/\mathrm V$, $\mathrm H=\mathrm T\,\mathrm m^2/\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm S=\mathrm A/\mathrm V$; these make the three displayed relations dimensionally consistent. Local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.

**(c) [Causal memory branch]** Alternatively, at each fixed material position $x$, declare a bounded continuous full history $E_x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and its response $P_x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Write $E(t)=E_x(t)$ and $P(t)=P_x(t)$ in the following formula; any field on a smaller time interval uses a declared full-history extension, not unspecified past values. The polarisation response is the causal convolution

$$P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)\,E(t-s)\,ds$$

for a declared real matrix kernel $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and units $\mathrm s^{-1}$; the integral then converges absolutely because $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$. The convolution uses only the past history; its continuity and causality are proved in `pthm-em-causal-dispersive-response`, while passivity is an additional model condition. Spatial or temporal differentiability of the resulting fields requires separate hypotheses when used. A finitely-subtracted analytic response may instead be declared by a dimensionless scalar transfer function $\chi$ that is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on the real boundary away from a real subtraction point $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfies $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ outside a compact set for some integer $n\ge1$ and constant $C>0$ ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Here $z,\omega_0$ are numerical angular frequencies in $\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the growth bound uses those SI numerical coordinates. Require also $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, hence $\chi(0)\in\mathbb R$, so that the response is defined on real harmonic histories independently of their representation. For $\omega\ne0$ the amplitude at that frequency is unique and reversing frequency conjugates it; the symmetry gives the same real output. At $\omega=0$ only $\operatorname{Re}e$ determines the input, and real $\chi(0)$ makes the output depend only on that input. For $e\in\mathbb C^3$, real $\omega$, and componentwise real part, declaring this transfer means adopting the harmonic relation $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})\mapsto P(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e e^{-i\omega t})$; upper-half-plane holomorphy alone does not construct a time-domain response for arbitrary histories.

**(d) [Status]** These are adopted model assumptions, one branch at a time; the framework does not derive them from the vacuum equations or from coarse graining, and no microscopic mechanism, material data or empirical validity is claimed. Ferroelectric and ferromagnetic response, hysteresis, nonlinear response and general nonlocal response lie outside the branches declared here.

(c) [Index restrictions] For $m=n=0$ one has $

(e) [Scope] These are separated candidate modes of the declared lossless model; the theorem asserts no completeness, no uniqueness among fields with the same data, and no lossy, dispersive or open-end behaviour, and it assumes the PEC model of the definition, not the physical infinite-conductivity limit.

Let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$, $a,b>0$, $\omega>0$, $\beta>0$ with $\beta^2=\omega^2\varepsilon\mu-(\pi/a)^2>0$, and put $\omega_c:=\pi/(a\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu})$, $\theta:=\beta x_3-\omega t$. In the rectangular guide of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]] with cross-section $(0,a)\times(0,b)$, take the TE candidate of [[pthm-em-rectangular-mode-candidates]](a) with $(m,n)=(1,0)$, whose amplitudes are $$\tilde E=\bigl(0,\,i\omega\mu\tfrac{a}{\pi}\sin\tfrac{\pi x_1}{a},\,0\bigr),\qquad \tilde H=\bigl(-i\beta\tfrac{a}{\pi}\sin\tfrac{\pi x_1}{a},\,0,\,\cos\tfrac{\pi x_1}{a}\bigr).$$ Then the real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(\tilde Ee^{i\theta})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(\tilde He^{i\theta})$ are smooth, have $E_z=0$ (TE) with $E$ linearly polarized along $e_2$, satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations and the PEC wall conditions, and carry a half-sine standing profile $\sin(\pi x_1/a)$ in $x_1$ with a traveling wave in $x_3$. If $a\ge b$, then $\omega_c=\pi/(a\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu})$ is the lowest cutoff among all TE and TM candidates of the cited theorem (attained also by $(m,n)=(0,1)$ when $a=b$); the case $(m,n)=(0,0)$ is not a mode by the index restriction of the theorem.
